title: Junking with the wagon, a traffic cop's help, and the death of his friend
summary: The boys hauled boxes past a friendly traffic cop; then the sick friend died and Turner became a pallbearer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers

blocks.x: And then I go back to my friend's house that had the wagon and the horse. I say, "Well, let's go and hustle some more stuff...some more junk and stuff, and we gonna make us some money so we can buy us some ice cream cones!"

So we took the wagon. We took off. We had a policeman downtown used to directin' traffic all the time. Great, big tall man. He'd have to be about six...seven feet tall. Everybody loved him 'cause he was traffic...he was a traffic cop downtown. So we come through the wagon, he stop everybody, let us through with the wagon.
"How you boys doin' today?"
"We ain't doin' so good. We ain't got no...we cain't find nobody throw no boxes out."
So he says, "Go 'round...go behind this store here. Try your luck."

So we went back there. It was a wholesale place, and they had a whole lot of boxes back there. We beat the...we got back there lucky and beat the old regular junkman come by and pick up the junk...we beat him back there, so we loaded up our wagon. We come back out. He let us by...hold up all the traffic...let us by. So we went off to the junkyard and get rid o' our paper boxes an' stuff. 'Cause we had to tear 'em up and tie 'em together. Wasn't nothin' too painful. We jus'...we went along to it, just like it wasn't nothin'. We'd be lucky to make thirty cents. That be a lot of money. Thirty cents. A whole wagonload of paper. So we in the big time. We's makin' money.
Reel 1
So, later on, during the time when we was hustlin' junk an' everything, the little boy got sicker.
(End of Reel 1)
JOSEPH VERNON "BIG JOE" TURNER JAZZ ORAL HISTORY TRANSCRIPTION
Patricia Willard, Interviewer
Reel Two
Los Angeles, California
Reel 2

So, when we got through junkin' and beatin' our heads against the bush, hustlin' up boxes and stuff, the little boy got sick, and he died, so I was scared of him, so his mother said she wanted the boys in the neighborhood to be the pallbearers. So she called over to my house, you know.
My momma told me, so I cried...'cause he was a good friend. And then...
How old was he?
Oh, I guess he's around fifteen...sixteen years old. And then, we...uh...my mother tried to talk me into goin' and bein' a pallbearer.
Say, "No, not me. I ain't gonna be no pallbearer." She say, "Well, it's your best friend. You ought to go." So, "I think it over."

So, afterward, I was...thought it over, and I told her, "Well, I talked myself into doin' it." So I went with the rest of the boys, and it wasn't too bad. We was his pallbearers. And, after that, the mother had the wagon, and the horse was [yamping ???] Would I come over there and work the horse out sometime? Or she gonna get rid of it.
I told her, "No, don't get rid of the horse and wagon. No, no, no. Don't do that."
